title: The Tense Audit: Find Out If Your Team Stopped Bringing You Problems

sections.title: Run the Tense Test on This Week's Messages
prompt: Pull up your last 10-15 Slack/email questions from your team. For each one, mark it future/conditional tense ("Should we cut it this way?") or past tense ("We went with X, FYI").
What's the ratio? If more than half are past-tense, you're being informed, not consulted.
Pick one past-tense message. Rewrite what the future-tense version of that same question would have looked like if they'd trusted you with it earlier.
Check your meeting invites from this week: were you added while the analysis was still open, or after it was already in the deck?

sections.title: Audit the Last Five 'Small' Problems Someone Brought You
prompt: List the last five low-stakes questions or quick asks someone brought you. For each, how long did it take you to respond, and in what tone?
Did the person who raised each one ever find out how it was resolved, or did it disappear into your queue?

Think about the PM's date-filter question in the piece — a small ask masking a bigger decision underneath. Is there a 'small' question sitting in your inbox right now that's actually testing whether you're safe for the real one?
Name one small ask you answered too fast or too dismissively. What would a slower, more curious response have looked like?

sections.title: Check Your Own Mechanism
prompt: Recall the last time someone brought you a problem or a rough draft. Did you start asking questions, or did you start explaining/fixing before they finished the sentence?
Do you ever open with something like "ugh, good catch, thanks" before diagnosing — or does your first reaction always sound like a cross-examination?
Think of a colleague who prefaces requests with 'sorry, I know you're busy, but—'. What has your past response pattern taught them about the cost of asking you?
Write down your actual opening line the last time someone brought you something half-finished. Would you want to hear that line if you were them?

sections.title: Do the Repair (No Announcement)
prompt: Pick two or three specific people. Ask them directly: 'The last time you brought me something half-finished, what did I do that made it not worth it?'
Next time someone brings you something rough, commit to asking questions for the first ten minutes before offering a fix or opinion — write down what you asked instead of said.
Define your own version of 'the drafts get rougher over time' metric: what would it look like, specifically, for people to bring you earlier and messier work again?
Identify one problem you're currently being routed around on. What's the ten-foot walk you need to make happen again?

cta: Run the tense audit on your last 10 messages and reply with your ratio — I want to know how many people are consulting you versus informing you.
